l: Lycosura, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Lycosura has a circuit of walls and a few inhabitants. It is described as the oldest of the towns on earth, either on the mainland or on islands, and as the first town seen by the sun and the model for all mankind's town building.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Arcadians call Mount Lycæus Olympus or the Sacred Hill, and they say Zeus was reared there. They maintain that the mountain's Cretea, rather than the island of Crete, was the place where Zeus was reared, and they honor the Nymphs Thisoa, Neda, and Hagno in connection with this story.

l: Mount Lycæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Mount Lycæus contains the grove of Parrhasian Apollo, a temple of Pan, a Hippodrome, the bases of statues, an enclosure sacred to Lycæan Zeus, and the altar of Lycæan Zeus. Its Hagno spring generally has as much water in summer as in winter, and its highest ridge provides a view of most of the Peloponnese.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The Arcadians say Zeus was reared on Mount Lycæus, at a place called Cretea, by the Nymphs Thisoa, Neda, and Hagno. Lycæan Zeus receives secret sacrifices at an altar on the mountain, and a priest prays to him and performs a customary sacrifice when drought harms the land.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: Parrhasian Apollo, also called Pythian Apollo, has a temple on the eastern part of Mount Lycæus. During his annual festival, the people sacrifice a boar to Apollo the Helper in the market-place, carry it to his temple in a solemn procession with flute playing, and burn its thighs while consuming its flesh there.

l: enclosure sacred to Lycæan Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: People may not enter the enclosure sacred to Lycæan Zeus, and anyone who violates the prohibition is said not to live more than a year. Men and beasts inside it are said to have no shadow at any time of year, so a hunter outside cannot see the shadow of a beast that enters it.

l: altar of Lycæan Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXVIII.
s: The altar of Lycæan Zeus is a mound of earth on the highest ridge of Mount Lycæus, from which most of the Peloponnese is visible. Two east-facing pillars and ancient golden eagles stand in front of it, and sacrifices to Lycæan Zeus are performed there secretly.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Phigalia lies on a mostly precipitous hill and was attacked and captured by the Lacedæmonians, causing the Phigalians to flee. The exiled Phigalians went to Delphi, where the Pythian Priestess declared that they could return only with the aid of 100 picked men from Oresthasium who would die in battle. The men of Oresthasium joined the expedition, fought the Lacedæmonian garrison, and all died after driving out the Spartans, enabling the Phigalians to recover their town. The unit also describes temples and statues at Phigalia, including those of Artemis the Preserver, Hermes, and Dionysus Acratophorus.

l: Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: Phigalia lies on a hill that is mostly precipitous, with walls built on the rocks and a gentle ascent to the town. It was attacked and captured by the Lacedæmonians, but the Phigalians later recovered it. The town contains a temple of Artemis the Preserver, a gymnasium with a statue of Hermes, and a temple of Dionysus Acratophorus.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Lacedæmonians attacked Arcadia and invaded Phigalia, defeating its inhabitants and besieging the town. They captured Phigalia and either forced the Phigalians to leave under terms of war or allowed them to evacuate. Their garrison was later driven out by the men from Oresthasium.

l: Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Phigalians who escaped went to Delphi to ask the god whether they should return to Phigalia.

l: Pythian Priestess, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Pythian Priestess told the Phigalians that they had no hope of returning by themselves. She said that their return would be possible if they took 100 picked men from Oresthasium and those men were slain in battle.

l: Oresthasium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: When the people of Oresthasium heard the oracle given to the Phigalians, they competed eagerly to provide the 100 picked men for the expedition to Phigalia.

l: the 100 picked men from Oresthasium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The 100 picked men from Oresthasium joined the expedition to Phigalia and engaged the Lacedæmonian garrison. They all died fighting bravely, fulfilled the oracle, and drove out the Spartans.

l: Lacedæmonian garrison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Lacedæmonian garrison at Phigalia engaged the 100 picked men from Oresthasium. It was driven out by them, allowing the Phigalians to recover their native town.

l: capture of Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The capture of Phigalia occurred when the Lacedæmonians defeated the Phigalians in battle and besieged the town. It took place when Miltiades was chief magistrate at Athens, in the second year of the 30th Olympiad.

l: flight of the Phigalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The flight of the Phigalians occurred after the Lacedæmonians had nearly taken Phigalia by storm. The Phigalians evacuated the town, either on their own initiative or because the Lacedæmonians allowed them to leave under conditions of war.

l: Phigalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Phigalians were defeated and expelled from Phigalia by the Lacedæmonians. Those who escaped consulted Delphi and followed the oracle by obtaining 100 picked men from Oresthasium; after the men drove out the Spartan garrison and died, the Phigalians recovered their town.

l: oracle concerning the return to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The oracle declared that the Phigalians could not hope to return to Phigalia by themselves. It promised their return if they took 100 picked men from Oresthasium and those men were slain in battle.

l: expedition to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The expedition to Phigalia was undertaken by the 100 picked men from Oresthasium together with the Phigalians' effort to recover their town. The men engaged the Lacedæmonian garrison, died fighting bravely, and fulfilled the oracle.

l: battle at Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: In the battle associated with the recovery of Phigalia, the 100 picked men from Oresthasium fought the Lacedæmonian garrison. All 100 were killed, but they drove out the Spartans and made the return of the Phigalians possible.

l: return of the Phigalians to Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XXXIX.
s: The Phigalians' return became possible after the 100 picked men from Oresthasium drove out the Lacedæmonian garrison and died in battle. The Phigalians thereby recovered their native town.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Phigalia has a stone statue of Arrhachion the pancratiast in its market-place, and its inscription has been obliterated. Arrhachion won twice at Olympia in the two Olympiads before the 54th, and the people of Elis awarded him a posthumous victory after he died while defeating his last opponent. The text also recounts how Creugas died in a boxing match with Damoxenus after they agreed to strike once in turn. The Argives awarded Creugas the victory at Nemea and erected a statue to him in Argos because Damoxenus violated their agreement.

l: Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Phigalia has the stone statue of Arrhachion in its market-place. Its people said that the statue once had an inscription, but time had obliterated it.

l: Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Arrhachion was a pancratiast who won two victories at Olympia in the two Olympiads before the 54th. In his final contest, he broke his opponent's finger but died while being throttled; he was nevertheless proclaimed victor.

l: statue of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The statue of Arrhachion stands in the market-place of Phigalia. It is an antique stone statue with feet not very widely separated and hands by the sides near the buttocks; its inscription has been obliterated.

l: Olympia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Olympia was the site of two of Arrhachion's victories in the two Olympiads before the 54th.

l: Olympic victories of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Arrhachion had two victories at Olympia in the two Olympiads before the 54th, attributed to the equity of the umpires and his own merit. In his last contest, the people of Elis awarded him victory after his death.

l: opponent of Arrhachion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Arrhachion's last opponent seized him with his feet and tightly grappled his neck with his arms. Arrhachion broke the opponent's finger, while the opponent throttled Arrhachion and then fainted from the pain in his finger.

l: Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Elis was associated with the umpires whose equity helped establish Arrhachion's earlier victories at Olympia.

l: people of Elis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The people of Elis crowned Arrhachion's dead body and proclaimed him victor after his opponent had fainted.

l: Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: The Argives awarded the dead Creugas the victory at Nemea because Damoxenus had violated the mutual agreement governing their boxing match. They also erected a statue to Creugas in Argos.

l: Creugas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Creugas was a boxer from Epidamnus who died after Damoxenus struck him under the ribs and tore out his bowels. The Argives nevertheless awarded him victory at Nemea and erected a statue to him in Argos.

l: Nemea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Nemea was the place where the Argives awarded Creugas the crown and victory despite his death.

l: Damoxenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Damoxenus was a Syracusan boxer who violated his agreement with Creugas to strike only once in turn. He was driven off the course after killing Creugas with a blow that tore out his bowels.

l: boxing match between Creugas and Damoxenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Creugas and Damoxenus agreed before the audience to strike one another once in turn because evening had come. Creugas struck Damoxenus's head first, but Damoxenus delivered a single hand blow under the ribs that pierced Creugas's side, seized his bowels, and tore them out; the Argives judged Damoxenus to have violated the conditions because he gave several blows instead of one.

l: Argos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XL.
s: Argos had a statue of Creugas, which stood in the temple of Lycian Apollo.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The Phigalians maintain a mortuary chapel for 100 picked men from Oresthasium and annually offer them funeral sacrifices as heroes. The rivers Lymax and Neda flow near Phigalia, and the Lymax joins the Neda near hot baths and the temple of Eurynome. The Phigalians identify Eurynome with Artemis, while their Antiquarians identify her as Oceanus’s daughter. On Mount Cotilius stands the temple of Apollo the Helper at Bassae, built by Ictinus, along with a roofless temple of Aphrodite.

l: Phigalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The Phigalians have a mortuary chapel in their market-place for 100 picked men from Oresthasium and annually offer them funeral sacrifices as heroes. They identify Eurynome as a title of Artemis and annually open her temple for public and private sacrifices.

l: Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Phigalia lies near the rivers Lymax and Neda and is surrounded on the left by Cotilius and on the right by the projecting mountain Elaion. About 12 stades from Phigalia are hot baths, and about 40 stades away on Cotilius is Bassae and the temple of Apollo the Helper.

l: Lymax, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The Lymax flows by Phigalia and falls into the Neda near the hot baths. The Phigalians say it received its name from the purifications of Rhea, and its course is described as second only to the Maeander in winding.

l: Neda, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The Neda rises on Mount Cerausius, part of Mount Lycaeus, and flows into the sea, where it is navigable for small craft. The Lymax joins it near the temple of Eurynome.

l: temple of Eurynome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The temple of Eurynome stands where the Lymax and Neda join, in rough and difficult country surrounded by many cypresses. It remains shut except on one day each year, when the Phigalians perform public and private sacrifices.

l: Eurynome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The Phigalians believe Eurynome to be a title of Artemis, while their Antiquarians say she was the daughter of Oceanus who joined Thetis in receiving Hephaestus. Her statue is said to be a woman down to the waist and a fish below, with gold chains around it.

l: Cotilius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Cotilius is a mountain about 40 stades from Phigalia and part of the surrounding landscape. It contains Bassae, the temple of Apollo the Helper, the place called Cotilum, and a spring whose water soon disappears into the ground.

l: temple of Apollo the Helper, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: The temple of Apollo the Helper stands at Bassae on Cotilius and has a stone roof. It is described as one of the finest temples in the Peloponnese, except for the temple at Tegea, and was built by Ictinus, who was also the architect of the Parthenon at Athens.

l: Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLI.
s: Apollo received the title Helper because he aided the Phigalians during a pestilence around the time of the Peloponnesian War. The text compares this title with his Athenian title Averter of Ill, which referred to turning away a pestilence from the Athenians.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The unit describes the cave on Mount Elaion sacred to Black Demeter and the traditions of the people of Phigalia about Demeter, Poseidon, and Despoena. It recounts how Demeter’s withdrawal caused the fruits of the earth to fail, and how Pan informed Zeus, who sent the Fates to persuade her to end her anger and grief. After an earlier statue of Demeter was destroyed by fire and the goddess’s rites were neglected, famine struck Phigalia, and the Pythian Priestess ordered the people to restore her honours. Onatas of Aegina later made a brazen statue of Demeter, but it had been crushed by falling stones before Pausanias’s visit.

l: Elaion, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Elaion is a mountain about 30 stades from Phigalia. It contains a cave sacred to Black Demeter.

l: Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Phigalia is associated with traditions about the amour of Poseidon with Demeter and the worship of Black Demeter. Its people neglected Demeter’s festivals and sacrifices after her earlier statue was destroyed, suffered a dearth, and later restored her honours and sacrifices.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: According to the people of Phigalia, Poseidon had an amour with Demeter, after which Demeter gave birth to Despoena.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Demeter gave birth to Despoena according to the people of Phigalia. After becoming angry with Poseidon and grieving over the rape of Proserpine, she dressed in black and hid in the cave on Elaion; the failure of the earth’s fruits followed until the Fates persuaded her to set aside her anger and grief.

l: Pan, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Pan traversed Arcadia while hunting in the mountains and saw Demeter dressed in black on Mount Elaion. He informed Zeus of her whereabouts.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Zeus learned from Pan where Demeter was hidden and sent the Fates to persuade her to abandon her anger and grief.

l: Phigalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The people of Phigalia believed that Demeter gave birth to Despoena after her amour with Poseidon. They placed a wooden statue of Demeter in the cave, later neglected her rites after it was destroyed, and then obtained a brazen statue from Onatas and renewed their worship.

l: cave of Black Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The cave of Black Demeter is on Mount Elaion near Phigalia and was considered sacred because Demeter had stayed there. It has a grove of oak trees around it and a spring where warm water bubbles up.

l: Onatas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Onatas of Ægina, the son of Mico, made a brazen statue of Demeter for the people of Phigalia after discovering a painting or copy of the ancient statue, possibly with additional guidance from a dream. He was a contemporary of the Athenian Hegias and the Argive Ageladas.

l: oracle at Delphi, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The Pythian Priestess served as the oracle consulted by the people of Phigalia when famine came upon the land.

l: the oracle's response, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The oracle's response told the Arcadians to go to the secret cave of the horse-bearing Demeter and seek relief from famine. It warned that they would soon eat one another and their children unless they appeased Demeter with public libations and restored divine honours to the cave.

l: wooden statue of Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The people of Phigalia placed a wooden statue of Demeter in the cave. It portrayed her seated on a rock with a mare’s head and mane, dragons and other monsters around her head, a tunic reaching to her feet, a dolphin in one hand, and a dove in the other; the statue later caught fire, and no one recorded its maker or the circumstances.

l: brazen statue of Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Onatas made a brazen statue of Demeter for Phigalia after finding a painting or copy of the ancient statue. Before Pausanias’s time, stones falling from the roof of the cave crushed and completely destroyed it.

l: the amour of Poseidon with Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The people of Phigalia believed the traditions about the amour of Poseidon with Demeter that were also told by the people of Thelpusa. They differed by saying that Demeter gave birth to Despoena rather than to a foal.

l: famine at Phigalia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: Famine followed the neglect of Demeter’s festivals and sacrifices after the earlier statue was destroyed. The people of Phigalia consulted the oracle, restored Demeter’s honours, and then resumed worship and sacrifices.

l: annual sacrifice to Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLII.
s: The annual sacrifice at Phigalia was conducted by a priestess and the youngest of the three citizens called Sacrificing Priests. It consisted of fruit of the vine and other trees, honeycombs, and unworked wool with its grease, all placed on the altar before the cave and covered with oil; no animal was sacrificed.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Pallantium was a town in Arcadia whose name was associated with the settlement founded near the Tiber by Evander and his Arcadian followers. The elder Antonine made Pallantium a town and granted it freedom and exemption from taxation, while also defeating the Mauri, taking territory from the Brigantes, restoring Cos and Rhodes, and supporting communities through financial and civic works. He was called Pius for honoring the gods and was praised for allowing certain subjects to leave their property to their sons rather than to the Emperor. His son Antonine later fought the Germans and subdued the Sauromatae after they began a war.

l: Pallantium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Pallantium was an Arcadian town associated with Evander and the Arcadians who founded a settlement near the Tiber. The elder Antonine made it a town and granted it freedom and exemption from taxation.

l: Evander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Evander was said to be the best of the Arcadians in council and war, and the son of Hermes by a Nymph who was the daughter of Lado. He led Arcadians from Pallantium to establish a colony near the river Tiber.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Arcadians accompanied Evander from Pallantium and formed a colony near the river Tiber. They inhabited part of what later became Rome, and that area was called Pallantium in memory of their town in Arcadia.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Arcadia was the region containing Pallantium, from which Evander and a force of Arcadians departed to establish a colony near the river Tiber.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Part of what later became Rome was inhabited by Evander and the Arcadians who accompanied him. The son Antonine fought against the Germans and subdued the Sauromatae in wars involving Rome.

l: Roman Emperor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The elder Antonine made Pallantium a town and granted it freedom and exemption from taxation. He drove the Mauri from their territory, took most of the Brigantes' territory after their attack on the Genunii, restored Cos and Rhodes after an earthquake, and supported needy Greeks and barbarians and public works.

l: Roman Empire, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Roman Empire, through the elder Antonine, granted Pallantium privileges because of its association with Evander and the Arcadian settlement near the Tiber.

l: tax exemption of Pallantium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The tax exemption of Pallantium was granted by the elder Antonine when he made Pallantium a town. The privilege made it free and exempt from taxation.

l: Mauri, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Mauri were described as the most important tribe of independent Libyans, as Nomads, and as more formidable than the Scythians because they and their wives rode horses instead of traveling in wagons. The elder Antonine drove them from all their territory into remote parts, including Mount Atlas and its neighbourhood.

l: Mauri war with Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Mauri war with Rome began when the Mauri commenced hostilities against Rome. The elder Antonine responded by driving them from their territory and compelling them to withdraw toward Mount Atlas and the area around it.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The elder Antonine gave grants of money to Greeks and barbarians who needed assistance. Some subject nations with Roman citizenship but whose sons were reckoned as Greeks were also affected by his change to the inheritance rule.

l: inheritance law favoring the Emperor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The inheritance law favoring the Emperor required certain Roman citizens whose sons were reckoned as Greeks either to leave their money to unrelated people or to let it increase the Emperor's wealth. Antonine allowed them to leave their property to their sons instead.

l: Antonine's philanthropy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Antonine's philanthropy included allowing eligible citizens to leave property to their sons rather than increasing the Emperor's wealth. He also gave money to needy Greeks and barbarians and supported magnificent works in Greece, Ionia, Carthage, and Syria.

l: Pius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: Pius was the title the Romans gave the elder Antonine because of the honour he paid to the gods. The text says he might also justly have been called the elder Cyrus or Father of mankind.

l: son Antonine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The son Antonine succeeded the elder Antonine. He fought against the Germans and subdued the Sauromatae after they began what the text calls an iniquitous war.

l: Germans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Germans were described as the most numerous and warlike barbarians in Europe. The son Antonine fought against them.

l: Sauromatae, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Sauromatae commenced an iniquitous war and were subdued by the son Antonine.

l: war between the son Antonine and the Germans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The war between the son Antonine and the Germans involved the son Antonine fighting against the Germans, who were described as the most numerous and warlike barbarians in Europe.

l: Sauromatae's war with Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIII.
s: The Sauromatae's war with Rome was described as an iniquitous war that they commenced. The son Antonine subdued them.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: The account of Arcadia describes roads and landmarks connecting Megalopolis, Pallantium, Tegea, and Asea. The Alpheus and Eurotas flow together for about 20 stades before disappearing and reemerging in different regions. Pallantium contains temples, statues, and the remains of an ancient citadel, while the Mound marks the boundary between the districts of Megalopolis, Tegea, and Pallantium. The route toward Tegea includes the temple of Aphneus and the well of Leuconius.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: Arcadia is described through roads, towns, rivers, temples, and ancient ruins, including places connected with Megalopolis, Pallantium, Tegea, and Asea.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: Megalopolis is connected by road with Pallantium and Tegea, and the road passes through its suburb Ladocea. The Alpheus reemerges at Pegæ in Megalopolis after flowing underground with the Eurotas.

l: Pallantium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: Pallantium lies beyond the Mound on the left-hand road and has a temple, stone statues of Pallas and Evander, and a temple to Proserpine. Its hill once served as the citadel and still contains remains of a temple of the gods called Pure, and a statue of Polybius stands nearby.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: Tegea shares a district boundary at the Mound with Megalopolis and Pallantium, and the Manthuric plain lies on its borders about 50 stades from the city. Near the road to Tegea are the temple of Aphneus and the well of Leuconius.

l: the Mound, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: The Mound is a boundary for the districts of Megalopolis, Tegea, and Pallantium. Roads turn from it toward the plain of Pallantium and the Manthuric plain.

l: Asea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: Asea lies about 20 stades from Athenæum and retains remains of walls on the hill that formerly served as its citadel. About five stades from Asea are the Alpheus, the source of the Eurotas, and a roofless temple of the Mother of the Gods; a road from Asea also leads to Mount Boreum.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: The Alpheus flows near Asea, a little away from the road, and has a source near a roofless temple of the Mother of the Gods. It joins the Eurotas, flows with it for about 20 stades, disappears into a cavity, and reemerges at Pegæ in Megalopolis.

l: the Eurotas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIV.
s: The source of the Eurotas is near the road about five stades from Asea. It joins the Alpheus and flows with it underground before reemerging in Laconia.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Tegea was said to have received its name from Tegeates, son of Lycaon, and its town was founded in its later form by Aleus. The Tegeans were renowned for Ancæus's and Atalanta's exploits against the Calydonian boar, Echemus's victory over Hyllus, and their defeat and capture of Lacedæmonians. Tegea's earlier temple of Athene Alea burned down, and the later temple was built on a larger and more magnificent scale. Scopas the Parian was identified as the architect of the new temple, whose sculptures depicted the Calydonian boar hunt and the combat between Telephus and Achilles.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Tegea was said to have received its name in the days of Tegeates, son of Lycaon, and its inhabitants were originally distributed among eight parishes, with a ninth, Aphidas, added during the reign of Aphidas. Aleus founded the town in its later form. Its great temple of Athene Alea was rebuilt after the earlier temple was destroyed by fire.

l: Aleus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Aleus was the founder of the town of Tegea in its later form. He also built the ancient temple of Athene Alea.

l: Calydonian boar, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: The Calydonian boar was attacked by Ancæus, who sustained its attack despite being wounded, while Atalanta was the first to hit it with an arrow. Its hunting was represented on one gable of the temple of Athene Alea.

l: Atalanta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Atalanta shot at the Calydonian boar and was the first to hit it. As a reward for this prowess, she received the boar's head and hide as trophies, and she was represented on the temple's gable among the hunters.

l: Tegeans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: The Tegeans shared in the common Arcadian wars against Ilium and the Persians and in the battle with the Lacedæmonians at Dipæa. They were the first Arcadians to defeat Lacedæmonians who fought against them and took most of them captive.

l: Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Athene Alea had an ancient temple at Tegea built by Aleus. After that temple was destroyed by fire, the people of Tegea built her a great and magnificent replacement.

l: great temple of Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: The great temple of Athene Alea at Tegea surpassed all temples in the Peloponnese in beauty and size. Its first row of pillars was Doric, its second row Corinthian, and its outer pillars Ionic; its gables depicted the Calydonian boar hunt and the single combat between Telephus and Achilles.

l: Scopas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLV.
s: Scopas the Parian was identified as the architect of the great temple of Athene Alea. He also made statues in various parts of old Greece, Ionia, and Caria.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVI.
s: The ancient statue of Athene Alea and the tusks of the Calydonian boar were carried away by Emperor Augustus after his victory over Antony and his allies, including the Arcadians except the Mantineans. The text says Augustus followed a long-established custom of removing votive offerings and statues from conquered nations. The statue of Athene Alea was later placed in Augustus's Forum at Rome, made entirely of ivory by Endœus. One tusk of the boar was said to have been broken off, while the remaining tusk was kept as a votive offering in Cæsar's gardens in the temple of Dionysus.

l: Athene Alea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVI.
s: The ancient statue of Athene Alea was carried away by Emperor Augustus after his victory over Antony and his allies. It was later displayed in the Forum at Rome built by Augustus, was entirely made of ivory, and was the workmanship of Endœus.

l: Augustus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVI.
s: Emperor Augustus carried away the statue of Athene Alea and the tusks of the Calydonian boar after his victory over Antony and his allies. He was said to have followed a long-established custom of carrying off votive offerings and statues from conquered nations, and he displayed the statue of Athene Alea in his Forum at Rome.

l: custom of carrying off votive offerings and statues, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVI.
s: The custom of carrying off votive offerings and statues from conquered nations was described as long-established and practiced by both Greeks and barbarians. The text gives examples involving the Greeks after the capture of Ilium, Antiphemus, Xerxes, Seleucus, the Argives at Tiryns, and the people of Cyzicus and Proconnesus.

l: victory of Augustus over Antony and his allies, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVI.
s: After his victory over Antony and his allies, among whom were all the Arcadians except the Mantineans, Augustus carried away the ancient statue of Athene Alea and the tusks of the Calydonian boar.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: At Tegea, the statue of Athene called Hippia by the Manthurii and Alea by other Greeks stands with statues of Æsculapius and Hygiea by Scopas. The temple of Athene contains ancient votive offerings, an altar attributed to Melampus, and representations of several divine figures, while games called Aleæa and Halotia are held nearby. Tegea also has a temple to Athene Poliatis, said to protect the city through a lock of Medusa’s hair given to Cepheus. The unit further recounts legends concerning Auge and Artemis Hegemone, whose dream-inspired intervention led Chronius to kill Aristomelidas and build a temple at Tegea.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: Athene is called Hippia by the Manthurii because they say she drove the chariot of Enceladus in the battle between the gods and giants; other Greeks and Peloponnesians call her Alea. Her altar at Tegea is said to have been made by Melampus and bears representations of Rhea, the Nymph Œnoe with Zeus as a baby, eight Nymphs, the Muses, and Mnemosyne.

l: statue of Athene at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: The statue of Athene at Tegea is called Hippia by the Manthurii and Alea by other Greeks and Peloponnesians, and it was taken from the Manthurii. Æsculapius stands on one side of it and Hygiea on the other, both made by the Parian Scopas in Pentelican marble.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: Tegea has temples to Athene Alea, Athene Poliatis, and Artemis, as well as a race-course where the Aleæa and Halotia games are held. It also has a spring associated with the violation of Auge by Hercules and a temple of Hermes Æpytus about three stades from the spring.

l: temple of Athene at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: The temple contains the hide of the Calydonian boar, rusty fetters once worn by Lacedæmonian captives, the bed of Athene, an effigy of Auge, and the armour of Marpessa. It also contains statues of the Muses and Mnemosyne, and its altar is said to have been made by Melampus.

l: Auge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: Auge is represented by an effigy in the temple of Athene at Tegea in imitation of a painting. A spring north of the temple is said to be the place where Hercules violated her, though the Tegean legend differs from Hecatæus’s account.

l: temple of Athene Poliatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: The temple of Athene Poliatis at Tegea is entered by its priest once each year and is called the temple of Protection. It is said to have been granted by Athene to Cepheus, son of Aleus, and to protect Tegea from capture through a lock of Medusa’s hair that Athene gave him.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVII.
s: Artemis, called Hegemone, is said to have stirred Chronius in a dream against Aristomelidas, the ruler of Orchomenus. After Chronius killed Aristomelidas and fled to Tegea, he built a temple there to Artemis.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The market-place at Tegea contains temples, statues, pillars, altars, and tombs connected with Aphrodite, Ares, Zeus, Tegeates, Mæra, Ilithyia, Polybius, and Elatus. Iasius is commemorated as the winner of the horserace at Olympia when Hercules established the Olympian games, and the passage explains the prizes and the origin of the palm-crown custom. The women of Tegea defeated the Lacedæmonians during the first invasion of Charillus, and their victory led to the worship of Ares Gynæcothœnas and a separate sacrifice by the women. The passage also records traditions about Auge’s delivery of Telephus at the temple of Ilithyia and his exposure and nursing on Mount Parthenium.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Tegea has a market-place containing temples, statues, pillars, altars, and tombs. Its women are said to have defeated the Lacedæmonians during the first invasion of Charillus.

l: market-place at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The market-place is shaped very much like a brick. It contains the temple and statue of the Brick Aphrodite, pillars commemorating legislators and Iasius, a statue of Ares Gynæcothœnas, an altar and statue of Adult Zeus, the tombs of Tegeates and Mæra, and the temple of Ilithyia.

l: Brick Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The Brick Aphrodite is worshipped in a temple in the market-place at Tegea, where there is also a stone statue of the goddess.

l: Iasius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Iasius is represented on a pillar in the market-place, with his left hand on a horse and a branch of palm in his right hand. He is said to have won the horserace at Olympia when Hercules the Theban established the Olympian games.

l: Olympia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: At Olympia, Iasius is said to have won the horserace when Hercules the Theban established the Olympian games. A crown of wild olive was given to the victor there.

l: Olympian games, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The Olympian games were established by Hercules the Theban. Their horserace was won by Iasius, and the prize at Olympia was a crown of wild olive.

l: Theseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: When returning from Crete, Theseus is said to have instituted games to Apollo at Delos and to have crowned the victors with palm. This is given as the origin of the custom of using the palm as a prize or emblem of victory.

l: Delos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Theseus is said to have instituted games to Apollo at Delos when he was returning from Crete. He crowned the victors with palm.

l: Ares Gynæcothœnas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Ares Gynæcothœnas has a statue on a pillar in the market-place at Tegea. The name means “Women’s Feast” and refers to the women’s separate sacrifice after their victory over the Lacedæmonians.

l: Laconian war, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: During the Laconian war, at the first invasion led by Charillus, the women took up arms and ambushed the Lacedæmonians under the hill later called Phylactris. The women helped cause the Lacedæmonian rout.

l: Charillus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Charillus, king of the Lacedæmonians, led the first invasion of Tegea in the Laconian war. He was captured and released without ransom after swearing that he would never again lead a Lacedæmonian army to Tegea, though he later violated the oath.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The Lacedæmonians fought the people of Tegea in the first invasion led by Charillus. They were routed after the women appeared in the battle, and Charillus was captured.

l: women of Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The women of Tegea took up arms and lay in ambush under the hill called Phylactris during the first invasion of Charillus. They appeared during the battle, helped cause the rout of the Lacedæmonians, and sacrificed privately to Ares without sharing the victim’s flesh with the men.

l: Marpessa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Marpessa, called the Widow, excelled all the other women in daring during the battle against the Lacedæmonians.

l: women's sacrifice to Ares, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: After the victory over the Lacedæmonians, the women privately sacrificed to Ares independently of the men. They gave none of the flesh of the victim to the men, which is why Ares was called Gynæcothœnas, or “Women’s Feast.”

l: Tegeates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Tegeates, the son of Lycaon, has a tomb in the market-place at Tegea.

l: Mæra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Mæra, the wife of Tegeates, has a tomb in the market-place at Tegea. She is said to have been the daughter of Atlas and is mentioned by Homer in Odysseus’ account of the souls he saw in Hades.

l: Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Ilithyia is associated with the temple in the market-place where Auge is represented on her knees. Auge is said to have given birth there, linking the place with Ilithyia.

l: temple of Ilithyia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: The temple of Ilithyia stands in the market-place at Tegea and contains a statue called Auge on her knees. One tradition says that Auge gave birth to a son on the spot where the temple now stands.

l: Auge, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Auge is represented on her knees in the temple of Ilithyia. One tradition says that Aleus ordered Nauplius to drown her in the sea, but that she fell on her knees and gave birth to a son while being led there; another says that she gave birth to Telephus secretly from her father.

l: Aleus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Aleus is said to have ordered Nauplius to take his daughter Auge and drown her in the sea.

l: birth of Telephus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: One tradition places the birth of Telephus at the spot where the temple of Ilithyia now stands, as Auge fell on her knees while being led away. Another tradition says that Auge gave birth to him without her father’s knowledge.

l: Telephus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLVIII.
s: Telephus is identified as the son born to Auge. In one tradition he was exposed on Mount Parthenium and suckled by a doe, a detail also recorded by the people of Tegea.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: The unit describes Philopœmen’s upbringing, character, education, and military career. After Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, Philopœmen led many of its inhabitants safely to Messene and later persuaded them to return with arms rather than accept Cleomenes’ conditions. He fought bravely at the battle of Sellasia, later improved the Achæan cavalry, and defeated the cavalry of Elis and the Ætolians at the river Larisus. The text contrasts Philopœmen’s hot temper with Epaminondas’ mildness and self-control.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: Philopœmen was the son of Craugis and was raised under the guardianship of Cleander after his father’s death. He was strong, devoted to farming, hunting, reading works on sophistry and strategy, and modeling himself on Epaminondas, though he was hot-tempered rather than mild. After Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, he safely led two-thirds of the adult citizens and all the women and children to Messene, persuaded the exiles to return with arms, fought bravely at Sellasia despite being pierced through both thighs, became a mercenary captain in Crete, and later made the Achæan cavalry the best in Greece.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: Epaminondas was Philopœmen’s model in character and military achievements. He is described as especially mild and as having complete control over his temper, qualities Philopœmen did not fully attain.

l: Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, prompting Philopœmen to lead many of its inhabitants to Messene. He later sent word that he regretted the capture and offered to let the people return if they signed a treaty, but Philopœmen persuaded them to return only with arms.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: Megalopolis was the home of Philopœmen and was captured by Cleomenes. Philopœmen evacuated two-thirds of its adult citizens and all its women and children to Messene, and later persuaded the exiles to return armed and without accepting conditions.

l: battle of Sellasia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: At the battle of Sellasia, the Achæans and Arcadians fought Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians, with Antigonus and a Macedonian army also taking part. Philopœmen shifted from the cavalry to the infantry when he saw that the infantry would determine the battle, fought with notable courage, and was wounded through both thighs before Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians were defeated.

l: Sellasia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: Sellasia was the site of a battle in which Philopœmen fought against Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians. The forces opposing Cleomenes included the Achæans, Arcadians from all the cities, and Antigonus with an army from Macedonia.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: The Achæans fought with the Arcadians and Antigonus against Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians at Sellasia. They later chose Philopœmen as commander of their cavalry, and their forces fought at the river Larisus against Elis and an allied Ætolian force.

l: cavalry of the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: After Philopœmen was chosen commander, he made the cavalry of the Achæans the best cavalry in Greece. Under his leadership it defeated the cavalry of the Ætolians and the men of Elis at the river Larisus.

l: battle at the river Larisus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER XLIX.
s: At the battle at the river Larisus, the Achæans and their allies fought the men of Elis and an Ætolian force supporting Elis because of kinship. Philopœmen personally killed Demophantus, the enemy cavalry commander, and then routed the Ætolian and Elean cavalry.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Philopœmen reformed the arms of the Achæan infantry and, as commander in chief, defeated the Lacedæmonians under Machanidas at the battle of Mantinea, killing Machanidas. He later gained honor among the Greeks, defended Megara against the Thebans, and forced Nabis to withdraw from Messene. Philopœmen also fought Nabis during the Roman war, setting fire to the Lacedæmonian camp at Gythium and defeating the Lacedæmonians in a night attack. Nabis later secured a temporary truce from the Romans but was assassinated by a man suborned by the Ætolians.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Philopœmen persuaded the Achæans to replace their short spears and oblong shields with breastplates, greaves, Argolic shields, and long spears. As commander in chief, he defeated the Lacedæmonians at Mantinea and slew Machanidas, later defended Megara, and compelled Nabis to withdraw from Messene. He went twice to Crete to help the Gortynians, fought Nabis near Gythium, and raised his fame by defeating the Lacedæmonians in a night attack.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: The Achæans left everything to Philopœmen and made him their leading figure. Their infantry adopted new armor, Argolic shields, and long spears at his persuasion, but their light-armed troops were beaten by the light-armed Lacedæmonians at Mantinea.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Lacedæmon was ruled by Machanidas and later by the tyrant Nabis, and it was involved in renewed war with the Achæans. Philopœmen's victories against its forces and the killing of Machanidas affected its political and military fortunes.

l: Machanidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Machanidas rose to power in Lacedæmon and led its forces against the Achæans. After pursuing the fleeing Achæan light-armed troops at Mantinea, he encountered Philopœmen and was slain by him.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: The light-armed Lacedæmonians defeated the light-armed Achæan troops at Mantinea, but Philopœmen routed their hoplites and killed Machanidas. Later, Philopœmen defeated and killed many Lacedæmonians in a night attack after setting fire to their camp at Gythium.

l: battle of Mantinea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: At the battle of Mantinea, the light-armed Lacedæmonians defeated the light-armed Achæan troops. Philopœmen formed his infantry into a square, routed the Lacedæmonian hoplites, and slew Machanidas as he returned from the pursuit.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Megalopolis was the home of Pylades, a noted harper who had won at the Pythian games. Philip sent men to Megalopolis to kill Philopœmen, but the attempt failed.

l: Nabis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: Nabis became tyrant of Lacedæmon and attacked the Messenians, taking all Messene except its citadel until Philopœmen arrived and compelled his withdrawal under conditions of war. He later fought the Romans, obtained a temporary truce from them, and was assassinated by a man who came ostensibly to negotiate an alliance but had been suborned by the Ætolians.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER L.
s: The Romans were at war with Nabis and equipped a fleet against him. Philopœmen wished to join their naval contest despite having no experience at sea, and the Romans and their allies remembered Homer’s description of the Arcadians’ maritime ignorance. The Romans later granted Nabis a truce for a definite period.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Philopœmen compelled the Lacedæmonians to join the Achæan League and later resisted Roman influence while reorganizing Sparta. As general of the Achæans, he exiled about 300 Lacedæmonian leaders, sold about 3000 Helots into slavery, demolished Sparta’s walls, and changed the youths’ training, though the Romans later restored their national training. After opposing concessions to Rome, Philopœmen led a small force into Messenia while ill, was captured, and was poisoned by Dinocrates. Lycortas then invaded Messenia, where the popular party joined him, those responsible for Philopœmen’s murder were killed, and Philopœmen’s remains were taken to Megalopolis.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Philopœmen compelled the Lacedæmonians to join the Achæan League and, although a private individual, shut the gates of Sparta against Titus Flaminius and Diophanes. He became general of the Achæans again, reorganized Sparta by exiling leaders, selling Helots, demolishing the walls, and changing the youths’ training, and later opposed concessions to the Romans. While suffering from a fever and aged more than 70, he joined Lycortas in Messenia, was wounded and captured, and was killed by poison on Dinocrates’ orders; his remains were taken to Megalopolis.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The Lacedæmonians were compelled by Philopœmen to join the Achæan League. They offered Philopœmen the house of Nabis, but he directed them to use their gifts to conciliate influential men in the Achæan League instead. During their impending civil war, about 300 leaders were exiled and about 3000 Helots were sold into slavery.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The Achæan League received the Lacedæmonians after Philopœmen compelled them to join it. Philopœmen was chosen general of the Achæans for a second time and later for an eighth time.

l: Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Sparta’s gates were shut against Titus Flaminius and Diophanes when they marched toward it. Philopœmen later ordered its walls demolished and its youths to train in the Achæan fashion, although the Romans subsequently restored the national training.

l: Lacedæmon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Titus Flaminius and Diophanes marched against Lacedæmon, alleging that the Lacedæmonians were plotting against the Romans. Philopœmen later permitted Lacedæmonian fugitives to return there after Manius had departed.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The Romans, commanded in Greece by Titus Flaminius, were alleged to be the object of Lacedæmonian plotting. They defeated Antiochus and the Syrians at Thermopylæ and later restored the Lacedæmonians’ national training.

l: Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The Achæans chose Philopœmen as their general for a second time and later for an eighth time. They sent Lycortas with an army to ravage Messenia during the dispute with the Messenians.

l: Manius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Manius and the Romans defeated Antiochus and the Syrians at Thermopylæ. He was willing to receive the Lacedæmonian fugitives, but Philopœmen opposed the proposal before the Council; after Manius departed, Philopœmen allowed the fugitives to return to Sparta.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Aristænus urged the Achæans to do whatever pleased the Romans and not resist them, but Philopœmen told him that he was hastening the fate of Greece.

l: Messenia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Messenia was the scene of a dispute with the Achæans and was ravaged by Lycortas’s army. Philopœmen was captured there and taken to Messene, and Lycortas later marched against Messenia after Philopœmen’s death.

l: Lycortas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Lycortas led an Achæan army to ravage Messenia and later marched against it with forces from Arcadia and Achaia. The popular party in Messene joined him, and those involved in Philopœmen’s murder were put to death.

l: Messenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The Messenians captured Philopœmen after he was wounded and had fallen from his horse. In their meeting, Dinocrates and the wealthy Messenians urged his execution, while the popular party sought to save him.

l: Dinocrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: Dinocrates and the wealthy Messenians urged that Philopœmen be put to death. He nevertheless had Philopœmen killed by poison and later committed suicide when Lycortas and the popular party acted against those responsible.

l: popular party, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The popular party in Messene wanted to save Philopœmen alive and called him the father of all Greece. It later fraternized with Lycortas’s forces, after which those involved in Philopœmen’s murder were put to death.

l: murder of Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LI.
s: The murder of Philopœmen was carried out when Dinocrates took him off by poison. After Lycortas marched against Messenia, those who were privy to the murder were put to death, except Dinocrates, who committed suicide.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: Greece ceased to produce a stock of distinguished men after Philopœmen, whom the text calls its last public benefactor. Miltiades is identified as the first public benefactor of all Greece, while Leonidas, Themistocles, Conon, Epaminondas, Leosthenes, and Aratus are also described in relation to Greece's defense or recovery. The leaders celebrated for the Peloponnesian War are said to have nearly ruined Greece, which Conon and Epaminondas later helped recover. An inscription at Tegea praises Philopœmen for his wisdom, bravery, victories over Spartan tyrants, and defense of freedom.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: Greece is said to have stopped producing a stock of distinguished men, with Philopœmen identified as its last public benefactor. It was nearly ruined by the most renowned leaders of the Peloponnesian War, then partly recovered through the actions of Conon and Epaminondas.

l: Miltiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: Miltiades, son of Cimon, defeated the barbarians who landed at Marathon and checked the Persian host. He is identified as the first public benefactor of all Greece.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, is identified as the last public benefactor of Greece. He is praised in an inscription at Tegea as a wise counselor, brave warrior, distinguished cavalry leader, victor over two Spartan tyrants, and abolisher of slavery.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: Epaminondas, son of Polymnis, helped recover Greece when it was in a pitiful state. He expelled Lacedæmonian garrisons and governors inland, put down the decemvirates, and added Messene and Megalopolis to Greece's importance.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: The Greeks were defended or aided by figures including Miltiades, Leonidas, Themistocles, Conon, Epaminondas, Leosthenes, and Aratus. Leosthenes brought 50,000 Greeks who had served for pay under Persia safely back to Greece by ship.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: The Persian invasion is represented by the barbarian landing at Marathon and by Xerxes' advance into Greece. Miltiades checked the Persian host, while Leonidas at Thermopylæ and Themistocles in two sea-fights expelled Xerxes from Greece.

l: Peloponnesian war, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: The figures who won the greatest renown in the Peloponnesian War are said to have nearly ruined Greece with their own actions.

l: inscription on Philopœmen at Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LII.
s: The inscription says that Philopœmen's fame and glory spread throughout Greece. It commemorates his wisdom in council, bravery in the field, eminence as a cavalry leader, victories over two Spartan tyrants, abolition of slavery, and defense of his country's freedom.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: At Tegea, Apollo and Artemis are said to have punished those who neglected Leto while she was pregnant and wandering through Arcadia. Apollo Aguieus and Artemis became associated with the killing of Scephrus by his brother Limon, the famine that followed, and rites performed at Tegea. The chapter also describes Tegean traditions about the migration of Tegeates’ sons to Crete, while noting that Cretan genealogies give different parentage for Cydon, Catreus, and Gortys. It records Tegea’s temples, altars, tribal statues, festivals, and surrounding sanctuaries.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Tegea has four statues of Apollo Aguieus, one erected by each tribe, and temples and altars dedicated to several deities. Its traditions include the annual festival at the place dedicated to Zeus Clarius, where Tegeans are said to have defeated invading Lacedæmonians after snow weakened them.

l: Apollo Aguieus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Apollo Aguieus is associated with the punishment of those who neglected Leto and with the death of Scephrus, whom Apollo privately addressed before Limon killed him. The people of Tegea erected four statues to Apollo Aguieus, and they honor Scephrus at his festival.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Artemis is said to have punished those who neglected Leto and to have killed Limon by shooting him with an arrow after he slew Scephrus. At Tegea, her priestess pursues someone during the festival of Apollo Aguieus while pretending to be Artemis pursuing Limon.

l: people of Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: The people of Tegea say that Apollo and Artemis punished those who neglected Leto in Arcadia, and that Tegeates’ sons Cydon, Archedius, and Gortys migrated to Crete. They maintain rites for Scephrus, possess four tribal statues of Apollo Aguieus, and preserve traditions about victories over the Lacedæmonians.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Arcadia is the region through which Leto wandered while pregnant, according to the tradition that Apollo and Artemis punished those who neglected her. Tegea’s people also maintain an altar called common to all Arcadians.

l: Scephrus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Scephrus, the son of Tegeates, privately conversed with Apollo when Apollo and Artemis came to Tegea. Limon mistakenly thought he was accusing him and killed him, after which the oracle at Delphi instructed the people to mourn for Scephrus.

l: Tegeates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Tegeates and Mera sacrificed to Apollo and Artemis after Limon killed Tegeates’ son Scephrus. Tegeates’ other sons are said by the people of Tegea to have migrated to Crete.

l: Limon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: Limon, the brother of Scephrus and son of Tegeates, mistakenly believed that Scephrus was making an accusation against him and slew him. Artemis immediately killed Limon with an arrow, and his pursuit is reenacted by the priestess of Artemis at Tegea.

l: festival of Apollo Aguieus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: At the festival of Apollo Aguieus, the people of Tegea pay honors to Scephrus. The priestess of Artemis pursues someone during the festival, acting out Artemis’s pursuit of Limon.

l: Crete, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIII.
s: The people of Tegea say that Cydon, Archedius, and Gortys migrated to Crete and gave their names to Cydonia and Gortys, as well as Catreus. The Cretans reject this account, instead giving Cydon as the son of Acacallis and Hermes, Catreus as the son of Minos, and Gortys as the son of Rhadamanthus; Crete is also associated with the stay of Dædalus at Minos’ court and with the work of Chirisophus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: The unit describes the boundary between the districts of the Lacedæmonians and Tegea, marked by the Alpheus, and traces the river’s unusual course through several regions before reaching the sea. It records roads from Tegea toward Thyrea and Argos, including temples, sacred groves, the supposed tomb of Orestes, and places associated with Pan, Telephus, and Dionysus. The road from Tegea to Argos crosses Mount Parthenium and reaches Hysiæ in Argolis, the boundary between Tegea and Argos. The text concludes by identifying these as divisions of the Peloponnese and listing the towns and notable things in each.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: Tegea is bounded from the Lacedæmonian district by the Alpheus. Roads from Tegea lead toward Thyrea and Argos, and the plain of Tegea is one place where the Alpheus disappears into the ground.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: The Alpheus rises at Phylace, receives another stream at the Meeting of the Waters, and disappears and reappears several times. After passing through Tegea, Asea, the districts of Pisa and Olympia, and beyond Cyllene, it is said to reappear at Ortygia in Syracuse and mix with the Arethusa.

l: Argos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: A high road leads from Tegea to Argos and passes temples of Æsculapius, Pythian Apollo, Demeter of Corythes, and Mystic Dionysus. After crossing Mount Parthenium, the road reaches Hysiæ in Argolis, identified as the boundary between the districts of Tegea and Argos.

l: Mount Parthenium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: Mount Parthenium lies on the road from Tegea to Argos. It contains an enclosure sacred to Telephus, who was said to have been exposed there as a boy and raised by a doe, and a nearby temple of Pan; it also has tortoises considered sacred to Pan and suitable for making lyres.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER LIV.
s: The unit concludes by referring to the divisions of the Peloponnese, including their towns and notable features.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Bœotia is contiguous to Attica, and Platæa to Eleutheræ; the Bœotians are said to take their name from Bœotus. The Platæans joined the Athenians at the battle of Marathon, fought with them after Xerxes's landing, and later helped repel Mardonius at Platæa. During the Peloponnesian war, the Lacedæmonians besieged and captured Platæa, and the Platæans were later restored after returning from Athens. The Thebans captured Platæa a second time three years after Leuctra, destroyed the town except for its temples, and Philip later restored it after his victory at Chæronea.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Bœotia is contiguous to Attica. The Bœotians are said to have received their name from Bœotus, son of Itonus and the Nymph Melanippe.

l: Platæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Platæans are thought to have been the original inhabitants of their land and to have taken their name from Platæa, who was probably the daughter of the king Asopus. They fought with the Athenians after Xerxes's landing, helped repel Mardonius at Platæa, were twice driven from their country, and were twice restored.

l: Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Athenians fought at Marathon with the Platæans and later took part with them in repelling Mardonius. They twice received the Platæans after their expulsion from Platæa.

l: Peloponnesian war, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: During the Peloponnesian war, the Lacedæmonians besieged and captured Platæa.

l: Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Lacedæmonians besieged and captured Platæa during the Peloponnesian war, blockading it with a double wall. They later occupied Cadmea, an action that the Platæans said they had neither proposed nor helped carry out.

l: capture of Platæa by the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Lacedæmonians captured Platæa during the Peloponnesian war after besieging and enclosing it with a double wall, which prevented the inhabitants from leaving.

l: Athens, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Athens received the Platæans after they were driven from their country, including after Platæa was captured during the Peloponnesian war.

l: Thebans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Thebans argued that the Lacedæmonians had brought about the peace and later violated it. Under Neocles, they approached Platæa by way of Hysiæ and Eleutheræ, captured the town, and required its inhabitants to leave before sunset.

l: Thebes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Thebes was the source of the force led by Neocles against Platæa. After Philip's victory at Chæronea, Philip introduced a garrison into Thebes.

l: second capture of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: The Thebans captured Platæa for the second time three years after Leuctra, when Asteus was Archon at Athens. They took the town while its inhabitants were outside the walls and required the people inside to leave.

l: destruction of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: After the second capture, the Thebans razed Platæa entirely except for its temples. There was no sack, and the Athenians again received the Platæans.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: After he was victorious at Chæronea, Philip introduced a garrison into Thebes and restored the Platæans as part of his efforts to destroy Theban power.

l: battle of Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: After the battle of Chæronea, where Philip was victorious, Philip introduced a garrison into Thebes and restored the Platæans.

l: restoration of Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, BOOK IX.--BŒOTIA. / CHAPTER I.
s: Philip restored Platæa after his victory at Chæronea and the introduction of his garrison into Thebes.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The unit describes the roads, ruins, tombs, monuments, and sanctuaries around Mount Cithæron, Eleutheræ, and Platæa. It discusses traditions concerning Mardonius, Actæon, Pentheus, and Œdipus, including Mardonius’s burial and Actæon’s death. Near Platæa, the Greeks maintain tombs for those who fell against the Medes, an altar and statue of Zeus Eleutherius, and the festival called Eleutheria. Within Platæa, the text describes a hero-chapel to Platæa and the temple of Hera, including statues of Rhea and Hera.

l: Mount Cithæron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Mount Cithæron contains the ruins of Hysiæ and Erythræ, the alleged tomb of Mardonius near the road, and traditions concerning where Pentheus met his fate and where Œdipus was exposed. It is sacred to Zeus of Cithæron.

l: Mardonius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Mardonius is associated with a tomb on the road near the ruins of Hysiæ and Erythræ. His body was missing after the battle, and different traditions identify who buried him; his son Artontes rewarded Dionysophanes and several Ionians for not neglecting his burial.

l: Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Platæa is reached by the road from Eleutheræ and has nearby tombs, a trophy, the altar and statue of Zeus Eleutherius, and the festival called Eleutheria. Within the town are a hero-chapel to Platæa and a temple of Hera.

l: Actæon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Actæon is said to have slept on a rock near a spring after hunting and to have seen Artemis bathing there. Stesichorus represented Artemis as dressing him in a deerskin so that his dogs would devour him, while the author believed madness came upon the dogs without the goddess’s intervention.

l: Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Artemis is said to have been seen bathing by Actæon at a spring near a rock called Actæon’s bed. Stesichorus represented her as dressing Actæon in a deerskin, although the author rejected the view that she caused the dogs’ madness.

l: Œdipus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: No one knows where on Mount Cithæron Œdipus was exposed after his birth. The text contrasts this uncertainty with the known crossroads on the road to Phocis where Œdipus slew his father.

l: Medes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Those who fell fighting against the Medes are commemorated by a tomb near the entrance to Platæa.

l: Greeks, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The Greeks have a common tomb near Platæa for those who fell against the Medes, while the Lacedæmonians and Athenians have separate burial-grounds. They also set up a trophy about 15 stades from Platæa for the battle there.

l: altar of Zeus Eleutherius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The altar of Zeus Eleutherius stands near the common tomb of the Greeks at Platæa. It is made of white stone, and the Eleutheria festival includes races in heavy armor held in front of it.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Zeus Eleutherius is honored at Platæa by an altar and a statue, both described as being near the tombs of those who fell against the Medes. The statue is made of white stone.

l: Eleutheria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Eleutheria is a festival celebrated at Platæa every fifth year. Its chief prizes are for running, with competitors running in heavy armor before the altar of Zeus Eleutherius.

l: temple of Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: The temple of Hera in Platæa is notable for its size and the beauty of its statues. It contains statues of Rhea and Hera, including a standing Hera called Full-Grown and a seated Hera called the Bride.

l: Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER II.
s: Hera is honored in Platæa by a large standing statue called Full-Grown and by a seated statue called the Bride. Both the Full-Grown Hera and the statue of Rhea are said to be made of Pentelican marble by Praxiteles, while the Bride is by Callimachus.

l: Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Hera, displeased with Zeus, went to Eubœa, so Zeus followed Cithæron's advice and staged a false marriage to Platæa using a dressed wooden statue. Hera discovered the deception, was pleased by the trick, and reconciled with Zeus, after which the Platæans commemorated the event with the festival called Dædala. The festival involved wooden images, processions from the Asopus to Mount Cithæron, and the burning of the images and animal sacrifices on a huge altar. The great festival was celebrated by communities throughout Bœotia, while the Platæans also held a smaller festival.

l: Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Hera was displeased with Zeus and went to Eubœa. She returned when she heard that Zeus intended to marry Platæa, tore the clothes of the wooden statue, recognized the trick, and reconciled with Zeus.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: When Hera could not be appeased, Zeus sought Cithæron's advice. He dressed a wooden statue as a bride and announced that he intended to marry Platæa, thereby prompting Hera's return and reconciliation.

l: Cithæron, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Cithæron, who ruled at Platæa and was known for his ingenuity, advised Zeus to use a dressed wooden statue and a wagon to make Hera believe that Zeus would marry Platæa.

l: Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Platæa was presented as the daughter of Asopus and was used as the supposed bride in Zeus's deception of Hera. The festival commemorating Hera's reconciliation with Zeus was associated with Platæa and the Platæans.

l: wooden statue (bride of Zeus), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The wooden statue was dressed as a young bride, placed in a wagon, and presented as Platæa in Zeus's false marriage plan. Hera tore its clothes when she discovered that it was only a wooden image.

l: Dædala, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Dædala was the festival commemorating the reconciliation of Hera and Zeus. Its name was connected with the old use of dædala for statues, and it included a smaller Platæan celebration as well as a great festival for all Bœotia.

l: Platæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The Platæans held a smaller Dædala in an oak-coppice near Alalcomenæ by identifying the tree on which a crow perched after taking boiled meat. They carved a wooden image from that tree, and at the great festival they decorated images, carried them to the Asopus, and brought them by wagon to Mount Cithæron.

l: oak-coppice near Alalcomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: The oak-coppice near Alalcomenæ contained oaks said to have the finest roots in Bœotia. At the smaller Dædala, the Platæans placed boiled meat there, watched the crows, and used the tree selected by a crow for carving the wooden image.

l: Bœotia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II, CHAPTER III.
s: Bœotia was the region whose communities joined the great festival of Dædala. The text says that the oaks near Alalcomenæ had the finest roots of all the oaks in Bœotia.
